info.bio: La historia Hootie comenzó en los apartamentos de estudiantes de la Universidad de South Carolina en el otoño de 1985. Un guitarrista flaco y alto de Maryland llamado Mark Bryan estaba saliendo de su cuarto cuando escuchó una increíble voz tipo barítono haciendo estragos en el pasillo. Preguntó a uno que pasaba si sabía quien estaba haciendo semejante música y se enteró que era Darius Rucker, quien también estaba estudiando periodismo como Bryan.

scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: La revolución iniciada en Chicago por Souled American y Uncle Tupelo (No Depression: baladas country con la furia del hardcore) se convierte en los noventa en un género propio: sus herederos abandonan el hardcore por los sonidos más espartanos y tradicionales. Son Volt de Jay Farrar y Wilco de Jeff Tweedy (Being There, Yankee Hotel Foxtrot); Will Oldham (Palace) arranca el movimiento; Freakwater, Ida, Handsome Family, Retsin, Blue Mountain, Whiskeytown, Grant Lee Buffalo, Citizens' Utilities, Willard Grant Conspiracy. El «chamber folk» de Lambchop, Lullaby For The Working Class, Geraldine Fibbers y Pinetop Seven; el country-rock de Volebeats, Ass Ponys, Sixteen Horsepower, Old 97's y los terroristas Grifters; el folk-rock de Swell, Counting Crows, Cracker, Cake, Hootie & The Blowfish; los Black Crowes; Belle And Sebastian, Arab Strap y los polacos Atman.

mentions.text: …Van Beethoven and Primus. Third Eye Blind looked for a middle path between hard-rock and folk-rock on Third Eye Blind (1997). A South Carolina band, Hootie & The Blowfish, which debuted with the charming Cracked Rear View (1994), was responsible with the Counting Crows for the continuing popularity of folk-rock.…

podcast.title: Creative Breakthrough with Jim Sonefeld (1989)
podcast.body: The band experienced a major creative breakthrough in the fall of 1989 when original drummer Brantley Smith left to pursue Christian ministry. He was replaced by Jim Sonefeld, a slightly older U of S.C. graduate who had played in goth-rock and classic rock bands and, crucially, was a budding songwriter. Sonefeld brought with him the song "Hold My Hand," which became a pivotal hit for the band. "The band's major creative breakthrough came in the fall of 1989, when original drummer Brantley Smith, uninterested in life on the road, amicably left the band to pursue Christian ministry. He was replaced by Jim Sony Sonafeld."

podcast.title: Early Demo EPs with Dick Hodgin (1990-1991)
podcast.body: In 1990 and 1991, Hootie & the Blowfish recorded two cassette EPs with Raleigh, North Carolina-based producer Dick Hodgin. These EPs served as demo tapes for the band and contained many of the songs that would later appear on their major label albums, including future hits "Hold My Hand" and "Let Her Cry," showcasing their early songwriting development. "In 1990 and 91, Hoody recorded two cassette EPs with Raleigh North Carolina-based producer Dick Hodgian that doubled as demo tapes for the band."

podcast.title: "Hacky-Sack Music in the Age of Flannel" (1991-1993)
podcast.body: During the peak of grunge from 1991 through 1993, Hootie & the Blowfish struggled to secure a major label deal because their mellow, melodic sound was considered out of step with the prevailing trend. As Tim Summer eloquently stated, "Hoody and the Blowfish were playing hacky-sack music in the age of flannel," perfectly capturing the perceived incongruity of their style during the grunge era. "Hoody and the Blowfish were playing hacky-sack music in the age of flannel."

podcast.title: Discovery by Tim Summer (1993)
podcast.body: Tim Summer, an A&R representative for Atlantic Records, discovered Hootie & the Blowfish at a gig in Charleston, South Carolina, in mid-September 1993. He was the only A&R person in attendance and was astonished to find a regionally popular band that was packing clubs across the Eastern Seaboard and had independently sold tens of thousands of CDs, realizing the immense potential that major labels had overlooked. "When he finally saw the band in mid-September, 1993 at a gig in Charleston, South Carolina, he was the only A&R guy in the crowd."

podcast.title: Financial Success as an Unsigned Band (1993)
podcast.body: Despite not being signed to a major label, Hootie & the Blowfish achieved remarkable financial success in 1993. They commanded between $5,000 and $10,000 per show and, combined with the 25,000 copies sold of their self-released *Kootchippop* EP, they earned over $300,000 that year. "Between that revenue and their live gigs, for which Hoody were now commanding between $5,000 and $10,000 a show, the band pulled down more than $300,000 in 1993 alone."

podcast.title: David Letterman's Career-Making Support (1994)
podcast.body: In the late summer of 1994, legendary late show host David Letterman happened to hear a Hootie & the Blowfish song on the radio and personally requested to book the band for his show, at a time when Atlantic Records was not even promoting them for late-night television. This appearance became the band's first national showcase, and Darius Rucker credits Letterman with making their career, as *Cracked Rear View* significantly climbed the Billboard 200 chart immediately following the performance. "To this day, Darius Rucker says quote, Letterman made our career, and we can never thank him enough."

podcast.title: Post-Letterman Chart Ascent (1994)
podcast.body: After their pivotal performance on the *Late Show with David Letterman* in late August 1994, *Cracked Rear View*, which had been languishing on the lower runs of the Billboard 200, leaped 30 places the following week and broke into the top half of the chart. By October, the album was in the top 50, and their single "Hold My Hand" had finally entered the Hot 100, marking the beginning of their gradual but steady ascent to national prominence. "The week after the Letterman performance, the album left 30 places, then broke into the top half of the chart the following week."

podcast.title: Best New Artist Grammy Win (1996)
podcast.body: In February 1996, the band won the coveted Best New Artist prize at the Grammy Awards. This achievement marked a significant peak in their early career, cementing their status as a major success, despite initial skepticism from critics and their label. "not only performing a track from their 12 times platinum album, but also winning statuettes, including the coveted best new artist prize."

podcast.title: Omission from 90s CNN Documentary (2017)
podcast.body: The band members, including Darius Rucker, Mark Bryan, Dean Felbert, and Jim Sonefeld, expressed mystification and hurt that a 2017 CNN documentary about music in the 1990s did not even mention them. This was despite the fact that their album *Cracked Rear View* was one of the decade's ten best-selling albums, suggesting a perceived lack of historical recognition for their massive impact. "said they were mystified and hurt, frankly, that a 2017 CNN documentary about music in the 1990s didn't even mention them, despite the fact that cracked rear view was one of the decades ten best-selling albums."

podcast.title: Celebration at Williams-Brice Stadium (2022)
podcast.body: In October 2022, Hootie & the Blowfish were still being celebrated at Williams-Brice Stadium in Columbia, South Carolina, during a college football game. The jumbo tron flashed Billboard chart data about *Cracked Rear View* and showed videos of the band, while thousands of students, faculty, and alumni swayed and sang along to Darius Rucker's voice, highlighting their enduring legacy as "favorite sons" of the University of South Carolina. "Throughout Williams' Bryce Stadium, thousands of students, faculty and alumni were swaying and singing along with Darius Ruckers' mighty baritone."

podcast.title: "Normcore" Aesthetic and "Beer and Gulf" Image
podcast.body: Hootie & the Blowfish were never considered "cool," even at the height of their popularity. Their aesthetic was described as "beer and gulf," and they "dressed Normcore before that had a name," suggesting an approachable, unpretentious image that might have contributed to their mainstream appeal but alienated some critics. "They were a band who dressed Norm Kor before that had a name, and their aesthetic was beer and gulf."

podcast.title: "Snoozy and the Bland Fish" Nickname
podcast.body: During the 1990s, many rock critics found Hootie's music to be mild, derivative, and inexplicably popular, leading some to jokingly refer to them as "snoozy and the bland fish." This critical perception contrasted sharply with their massive commercial success and hinted at a disconnect between critical acclaim and popular appeal. "I'll admit, in the 90s, I made my share of snoozy and the bland fish, jokes."

podcast.title: Anti-Nirvana Vibe and Organic Radio Success
podcast.body: Hootie & the Blowfish were perceived as having an "anti-Nirvana" sound or vibe during their rise in the mid-1990s. This appeal contributed to the organic success of their "I Go Blind" cover on radio, as DJs in cities like Boulder or Denver picked it up and fans requested it widely. "It was sort of the anti-Nurvana and people started requesting it."

podcast.title: Cover of "I Go Blind" by 5440
podcast.body: Hootie & the Blowfish covered 5440's song "I Go Blind." Although they had recorded it, it was cut from their first album. It later appeared as a B-side on a cassette single and was licensed for the "Friends" soundtrack. They specifically requested that it not be released as a single from the soundtrack. "They had recorded I Go Blind. It didn't make their first record. It was cut. But they said, you can have this song, but just promise us you won't release it as a single for the friend soundtrack."

podcast.title: Dominant Album Sales of the 1990s
podcast.body: Hootie & the Blowfish had the top-selling album of 1995 with *Cracked Rear View*, and it became one of the best-sellers of the entire decade. The album remarkably outsold contemporary records by bands like Pearl Jam, Toad the Wet Sprocket, and R.E.M., demonstrating their immense commercial success. "The band not only had the top selling album of 1995, but one of the best sellers of the decade, outselling any album by the bands that had paved the way for Judy, from Pearl Jam to Toad the Wet Sprocket to R&M."

podcast.title: Early Fandom of 5440 and R.E.M.
podcast.body: Before their rise to fame, Hootie & the Blowfish were avid fans of 5440 and R.E.M. They regularly attended 5440's shows at the 930 Club in Washington, DC, and, as a cover band, performed almost every song from 5440's "Green Record" and every R.E.M. song. "They're two favorite bands were REM and 5440 oddly."

podcast.title: Early R.E.M. Cover Band
podcast.body: For a period, especially when Darius Rucker and Mark Bryan expanded their act, Hootie & the Blowfish were largely an R.E.M. cover band. They incorporated up to 12 R.E.M. songs into their sets, demonstrating the profound influence R.E.M. had on their early sound and repertoire. "Quote, we were basically an REM cover band, Rucker told Summer. At one point, we were playing 12 REM songs in our set."

podcast.title: Frustrated Major Label Dealings (Early 1990s)
podcast.body: The band faced significant frustration in their attempts to sign with a major label. They initially turned down a deal with MCA-affiliated Gasoline Alley due to a handshake agreement with J.R.S. Records (an RCA affiliate). However, after traveling to Los Angeles in 1991 to formalize the J.R.S. deal, one of its lead executives disliked the band and pulled their studio funding, effectively nullifying the agreement. "Hoody's efforts to get signed to a major label were frustrating and almost comically ill-fated."

podcast.title: Impact on College-Friendly Bands
podcast.body: By riding the charts in the mid-1990s, Hootie & the Blowfish made the airwaves safe for a new generation of jangly and college-friendly bands. Contemporaries like the Dave Matthews Band, whose major label debut had just gone platinum, and Blues Traveler, who were finally scoring their first-ever top 40 hits, benefited from the sonic landscape Hootie helped create. "Riding the charts alongside Hoody by mid 1995 were the Dave Matthews band whose major label debut had just gone platinum. And Blues Traveler, who, after languishing for several albums, were finally scoring their first ever top 40 hits in 95."

podcast.body: When the band first consisted only of Darius Rucker and Mark Bryan, they were briefly known as The Wolf Brothers. This early incarnation pre-dated the formation of Hootie & the Blowfish as a full quartet. "By then, the band that was briefly known as The Wolf Brothers when it was just Rucker and Bryan had finally picked their name."

podcast.title: No US Airplay Royalties for Cover Songs
podcast.body: As an American artist playing a cover on American radio, Hootie & the Blowfish did not receive radio airplay royalties for "I Go Blind." These royalties are typically paid only to the composers and publishers of the original song. Their only benefit came from mechanical royalties (sales) of the "Friends" soundtrack or the cassette single. "if you are an American artist on American radio and you're playing a cover, you don't reap any radio airplay royalties from that because it only goes to the composers."

podcast.title: Origin of the Band Name
podcast.body: The name "Hootie and the Blowfish" originated from nicknames of two University of South Carolina students who were friends with Darius Rucker and were always seen together on campus. The band struggled to come up with a better name, even considering the rejected, racially charged option "Black and Blue" to denote their Black lead singer and three white band members, before settling on the now-famous moniker. "Hoody and the Blowfish were nicknames of two U of S C students, Rucker was friends with, who were always seen on campus together."

podcast.title: Positive Relationship with 5440
podcast.body: The band maintained a very positive relationship with 5440 following the success of "I Go Blind." They were genuinely happy for 5440's financial gain, toured together, and their drummer, Sony, made efforts to ensure 5440 received their due royalties. "The band were very, very happy for us. We did some tour with them... Sony was, came in with the billboard... he goes, you guys are going to get some money."

podcast.title: Pre-Game "Thing" at U of SC
podcast.body: The celebration of Hootie & the Blowfish's chart feats at University of South Carolina events, such as football games and local library talks, was a known "thing" at the institution, even 27 years after their peak. This indicates a sustained pride and cultural attachment to the band within their alma mater community. "This was, I discovered, a thing at U of S.C."

podcast.title: Record Label's Failed Attempt to Stop "I Go Blind" Airplay
podcast.body: Hootie & the Blowfish's record label attempted to halt the widespread radio play of "I Go Blind" in favor of their newly released official single. However, the new single "pretty well died" on radio, with stations opting to continue playing the popular 5440 cover. "They tried to stop it. I mean, they're new record just been released and they basically told Radio, look, shut that song down. Here's our new single. They released that single and it pretty well died."

podcast.title: Rehabilitation by John Karamanica
podcast.body: Recently, some critics, notably John Karamanica of *The New York Times*, have attempted to restore the band's standing in music history. Karamanica has been described as a "one-man Hoody rehabilitation machine," dedicating several podcast episodes to the band and arguing that their significance and musicality were undervalued. "Only fairly recently have some critics tried to restore the band's standing in music history."

podcast.title: Role in Mainstreaming Jangly Americana (Mid-1990s)
podcast.body: Hootie & the Blowfish were credited with leading the mainstreaming and mellowing of "jangly Americana" in the mid-1990s. Their success transformed what had been considered cutting-edge and postmodern R.E.M.-esque sounds in the 1980s into centrist rock and pop, effectively making the airwaves safe for a new generation of similar-sounding bands like Dave Matthews Band and Blues Traveler. "Some summers pet project was in the right place at the right time, leading the mainstreaming and mellowing of Djangly Americana."

"Judy and the Blowfish, a band formed at the University of South Carolina in the 1980s."

xref.body: "I Go Blind" was a track on the 1986 Green Album. When Hootie & the Blowfish covered it and included it on a Friends soundtrack compilation in the 1990s, it became a massive hit on American radio. The story of what happened with that song and its second life was presumably covered in Part 2 of the "In Their Own Words" series.
